title: REFACTOR-VLA: Unsupervised Library Learning of Typed Motor Programs
gist: Apple researchers introduce REFACTOR-VLA, a wake/sleep architecture that lets vision-language-action robot models discover reusable, typed 'skill' abstractions instead of generating raw motor commands, and show that naively scaling the world model backbone hurts performance while adding an auxiliary contrastive loss substantially improves skill discovery quality.

insights.claim: Current vision-language-action (VLA) models such as OpenVLA, pi0, RT-2, and RDT-1B are 'monolithic': they generate raw motor commands or very short action sequences without organizing behaviors into reusable, well-defined abstractions, which causes poor performance on long-horizon multi-step tasks and makes it hard to interpret what they have learned.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Points to a structural bottleneck in leading robotics/VLA model families that limits their use on complex multi-step robotic tasks, a gap that abstraction-learning approaches like REFACTOR-VLA are positioned to address.
insights.quote: Most current vision-language-action (VLA) models—such as OpenVLA, π0, RT-2, and RDT-1B—are “monolithic.”
insights.locator: Most current vision-language-action (VLA) models—such as OpenVLA

insights.claim: Existing skill-discovery methods sidestep the core problem of judging when two action sequences are 'behaviorally equivalent': AtomicVLA and AtomSkill cluster contrastive embeddings, while BLADE and LRLL rely on an LLM judge that is not calibrated to the robot's own dynamics.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Signals a methodological critique of the field's prior art that motivates REFACTOR-VLA's world-model-grounded equivalence kernel as a more principled alternative.
insights.quote: these LLMs are not calibrated to the robot’s own dynamics
insights.locator: Existing approaches for discovering skills often avoid the core problem

insights.claim: REFACTOR-VLA learns reusable robot skills via a wake/sleep architecture: in sleep, a Behavioral-Equivalence Kernel (BEK) built on rollouts from a learned latent world model (M-phi) clusters motor-program segments; in wake, the system generates typed lambda terms (inspired by the Hindley–Milner type system) that a library-conditioned rectified-flow action decoder turns into actions, with new skills accepted only if they pass both a Minimum Description Length (MDL) criterion and a return-preservation gate.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: A concrete architectural template for turning unstructured robot demonstrations into a typed, reusable skill library grounded in learned world-model dynamics rather than raw embeddings or LLM judgment.
insights.locator: We introduce REFACTOR-VLA, a system that learns reusable skills

insights.claim: REFACTOR-VLA is trained in three phases: Phase A warms up the latent world model M-phi, Phase B optimizes the wake-phase policy that uses the skill library, and Phase C runs sleep-phase clustering to discover new reusable skills from action fragments.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Defines a reproducible three-stage training recipe (world-model warmup, policy optimization, skill discovery) that others could adopt or benchmark against for library-learning robot policies.
insights.locator: To train REFACTOR-VLA, we use a three-phase schedule

themes.theme: LIBERO benchmark findings: bigger world model hurts, auxiliary loss helps

insights.claim: On the full LIBERO benchmark suite, increasing the latent world model's size from 188 million to 430 million parameters worsened performance on 4 out of 4 benchmark suites, disproving the assumption that a bigger world model always improves results.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: A concrete counter-example to naive scaling-is-better assumptions in world-model-based robot learning; investors and researchers tracking robotics/embodied-AI scaling narratives should note that parameter count alone is not a reliable lever here.
insights.quote: simply increasing the size of the world model—from 188 million to 430 million parameters—worsened performance on 4 out of 4 benchmark suites
insights.locator: We evaluated REFACTOR-VLA on the full LIBERO benchmark suite

insights.claim: Adding an auxiliary supervised contrastive loss (InfoNCE) during the world-model warmup phase (Phase A) greatly improved skill-clustering quality in the sleep phase (Phase C), yielding Normalized Mutual Information (NMI, n=3 multi-seeding) of 0.462±0.021 on the Object suite, 0.867±0.025 on Spatial, 0.915±0.013 on Goal, and 0.754±0.010 on LIBERO-10.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Identifies the training-objective choice (auxiliary contrastive loss), not model scale, as the key lever for better unsupervised skill discovery — a specific, testable finding for teams building similar library-learning robot policies.
insights.quote: adding an auxiliary supervised contrastive loss (specifically, InfoNCE loss) during the world-model warmup (Phase A) greatly improved the quality of skill clustering
insights.locator: Second, changing the training objective makes a big difference
